meta.title: Who really said "Never argue with an idiot. They drag you down to their level and beat you with experience"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not George Carlin. The line traces to advice Yul Brynner credited to Jean Cocteau in 1956; the modern wording surfaced anonymously on Usenet in the 1990s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never argue with an idiot. They drag you down to their level and beat you with experience'?
meta.ogDescription: Not George Carlin, and not Mark Twain. The oldest ancestor carrying the sting in the tail is a 1956 AP interview in which Yul Brynner credited Jean Cocteau.

answer.label: Not George Carlin — an anonymous 1990s rewrite
answer.authorDates: Oldest named claimant: Jean Cocteau (1889–1963), via Yul Brynner in 1956 — and not in this wording
answer.sourceLine: The saying was circulating for years before Carlin’s name attached to it: Matt Seybold found it in none of the George Carlin broadcasts, albums or books from the period it surged — 1998, the height of his fame — and the earliest Carlin credit on record is an October 2013 Usenet post, five years after his death. The oldest ancestor carrying the sting in the tail is advice Yul Brynner credited to his friend Jean Cocteau in a syndicated Associated Press profile of 13 November 1956 — in noticeably different words — while this particular wording first surfaces, unattributed, in Usenet posts of the 1990s. Per Quote Investigator ↗ and the Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually comes from

Daily Picayune, 28 April 1878 — “To argue with a fool is to make him your equal” (per Quote Investigator); Proverbs 26:4 earlier still

source.excerpt: Never associate with idiots on their own level, because, being an intelligent man, you’ll try to deal with them on their level—and on their level they’ll beat you every time.
trail: 13 November 1956 — Associated Press reporter Hal Boyle asks Yul Brynner for the greatest advice he has ever received. Brynner credits his friend Jean Cocteau with a line about never associating with idiots on their own level, because on their level they will beat you every time. The profile is syndicated across hundreds of American newspapers (Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗).

1958 — writing in the University of North Carolina student newspaper, columnist Frank Crowther conflates “associate” with “argue” — still crediting Cocteau. Quote Investigator ↗ dates that version to January 1958 in The Daily Tar Heel; the last appearance carrying the Cocteau credit that Seybold can find is the Kaplan Herald in 1987 ↗.

December 1993 and March 1997 — the modern shape surfaces on Usenet with no author attached at all: “Argue with idiots, they drag you to their level & win with experience,” then “Never Argue with idiots, They drag you down to their level, And beat you with experience!” These are the earliest drag–level–experience forms in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.

1998 onward — six American newspapers run it unattributed inside a single twelve-month period, it reaches Facebook by 2005 (Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗), Twitter starts crediting Mark Twain in June 2009, and the earliest George Carlin credit in Quote Investigator’s record ↗ is an October 2013 Usenet post — five years after Carlin’s death in 2008.
source.excerptNote: Yul Brynner’s answer when AP reporter Hal Boyle asked him what the greatest advice he had ever received was, 13 November 1956. He credited it to his friend Jean Cocteau. This is the earliest credible attribution Quote Investigator ↗ documents — and it is plainly not the sentence people quote today.

source.rightsNote: This wording has no identified author and no established first publication, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The 1956 Associated Press profile that carries its oldest documented ancestor is a mid-century news article whose own rights status we have not established; the sentence as it circulates today is an anonymous internet-era rewrite of uncertain ownership.

author.name: Jean Cocteau
author.heading: About Jean Cocteau
author.bio: Jean Cocteau was one of the twentieth century’s great cultural omnivores — poet, novelist, playwright, designer and film director, author of Les Enfants Terribles (1929) and of the films Beauty and the Beast (1946) and Orpheus (1950). He befriended Yul Brynner when Brynner was an unknown actor in Paris and opened the doors that made his career; Brynner later appeared in, and helped finance, Cocteau’s final film The Testament of Orpheus (1960). The aphorism reached print only through Brynner’s account of it in a 1956 interview — it has never been located in Cocteau’s own writings, so even this credit is a report rather than a citation.

misattribution.heading: Everyone has held this line except the person who wrote it
misattribution.intro: This is a saying that has changed hands repeatedly and lost its source along the way. The oldest documented version belongs to mid-century cinema; the modern wording belongs to nobody in particular.

items.why: Carlin died in 2008, and the sentence was already circulating for years before his name attached to it. Matt Seybold checked: it “does not appear in any of the George Carlin broadcasts, albums, or books from this period, the very height of his popularity” (Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗). Quote Investigator ↗ finds no substantive support for the credit and notes Carlin received it many years after the quip was in circulation. Carlin himself used his official website to disown material forwarded around the internet under his name — “Don’t blame me” (Wikiquote ↗).

items.scope: The most common credit of all
items.why: Twain died in 1910 and the attribution appeared decades later. Twain scholar Matt Seybold is unequivocal: “Mark Twain never said these words, nor anything resembling them” (Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗). Quote Investigator ↗ records tweets crediting Twain from June 2009 and a Goodreads entry by 2011.

items.who: Kevin Garnett, Scott Adams / Dilbert, Bob Gray
items.why: Seybold lists the basketball player Kevin Garnett among the celebrities the saying has been pinned on (Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗). Quote Investigator ↗ also logs a January 1999 Usenet joke list that filed the line under “Dilbert’s Words of Wisdom” — the strip is Scott Adams’s, though the post credits the strip rather than the man, and that 1999 list carries this page’s exact wording — and a September 1978 Memphis Press-Scimitar item crediting a Bob Gray, with the older “associate with idiots” wording, not the modern sentence.

Even the oldest named credit rests on one interview. Seybold reviewed Cocteau’s published writings and could not establish that the remark Brynner attributed to him appears anywhere except the Boyle profile — and observes that Brynner had a habit of invoking Cocteau as cover for his own off-colour lines (Center for Mark Twain Studies ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote this sentence. The idea is documented to at least 1956, when it was credited to Jean Cocteau; this particular wording is an anonymous internet-era compression, first recorded on Usenet in the 1990s (Quote Investigator ↗). George Carlin is simply the funniest available name to hang it on.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Carlin
lead: Carlin spent a career on exactly this terrain — one of his most quoted routines turns on how stupid the average person is, and half of everyone being stupider still — which is precisely why the line adheres to him. Attribution follows plausibility, not evidence: a cynical one-liner drifts toward the most famous available cynic, and Carlin, Mark Twain and (occasionally) the basketball player Kevin Garnett have all taken turns holding it.

What makes this case unusual is that the trail does not simply evaporate — it ends at a specific, checkable moment. On 13 November 1956 an Associated Press reporter asked one of the biggest movie stars in America what the best advice he had ever received was, and got back a Jean Cocteau aphorism about idiots. Everything after that is erosion: “associate” became “argue” by 1958, the Cocteau credit fell away by the late 1980s, and the internet reassembled the sentence into something punchier and handed it to whoever seemed to deserve it.
context.detailsSummary: The idea is much older than the joke
detailsBody: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the underlying thought back well past the twentieth century. Proverbs 26:4 warns against answering a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him, and by 1878 American newspapers were printing compressed secular versions: the Daily Picayune of 28 April 1878 ran “To argue with a fool is to make him your equal,” and the Rochester Evening Express followed in May with “Don’t argue with a fool, or the listener will say there is a pair of you.”

None of those is the modern sentence. What the twentieth century added was the sting in the tail — not merely that arguing with a fool lowers you, but that once you are down there, he has more practice than you do.
context.pull: “Don’t blame me.” — George Carlin, on writings falsely attributed to him online
